newsitem.title: UK: Holidays keep Europe grains market subdued.
newsitem.headline: Holidays keep Europe grains market subdued.

text.p: Holidays in the UK and Ireland on Monday and most of the north-western continent on Thursday have helped keep the European grains market subdued this week.
Steady rain knocked French grain prices especially on the southwest maize market where a variety of bearish factors were heaping up against recent prices, traders said.
A thoroughly soggy week across most of the country allowed maize sowings to resume and freshened crops already in the ground, though without doing much to fill depleted reservoirs.
Even as weather experts started talking in vague terms about the risk of flooding in some areas, new curbs on irrigation went into force in seven provinces, bringing the total to 25.

Maize fell about 20 francs a tonne at Bordeaux, as traders absorbed forecasts of a French surplus and the prospect of ample preferential supplies coming in from the United States to target markets in the Iberian peninsula.
Adjudications are due to begin in the next two weeks for new EU maize quotas for Spain and Portugal from the United States.

Traders reckoned a provisional allocation of 500,000 tonnes for Spain could be raised by as much as 300,000 tonnes due to recent drought damage in Spain, further shutting out French maize. There was no EU confirmation of this.
An outbreak of swine fever in Spain, though seen under control, has prompted pig slaughtering and so could cut demand.
Lower wheat prices also weighed on maize.
Those prices eased also in part due to the weather but a surprise EU decision to suspend a planned export tax had little effect with most old-crop positions now covered, traders said.

In the UK, still abundant old crop supplies are putting the market under pressure, traders said. "No-one wants to be left long at the end of the season," one trader said. "It's very cheap," he said, noting that old crop was at a discount to new.
This cheapness of UK wheat meant that there was still demand from Portugal and Spain, and one shipment went to Italy at the start of the week, traders said.
Farmers were starting to relent and bring more to the market. "The farmers have thrown in the towel," the one trader said.
Wet weather through most of this week has alleviated the immediate weather worries of farmers and traders, although a long term question remains over supplies for irrigation.
Activity on the German grain market ended the week muted after the holiday but also because old crop supply is thinning.
Large-scale new crop negotiations have not really started in wheat, but brokers point out farmers are ready to fix barley sales contracts at what is considered a cheap 250-255 marks cif.

One reason is the improving crop weather -- soil moisture levels are now fine and although temperatures are still low, the crops should be able to make a full recovery from any damages suffered during the cold and dry March/April period.
Traders also think farmers favour the retention of new crop wheat at the expense of barley because that is where they think the money will be.
Domestic and export prices have eased, but to a lesser extent than in other European countries where levels previously soared on far more serious drought conditions.
Brokers do not believe in a free-fall in spot prices in the weeks to come because supplies are limited.
New crop prices remain tied to weather prospects.
Spanish grains were static amid very light trade on Friday, although barley rose strongly on a lack of supply.
However barley is expected to weaken on expectations of a good harvest and maize prices were limp because of strong imports.
"Barley prices are being kept artificially high. As soon as we have the harvest we'll see prices falling," a trader said.
Conversely, wheat prices are expected to rise because the harvest in total is thought likely to be less than 1996.
Last year Spain produced 6 million tonnes of wheat, official data show.
"I think durum wheat prices will remain strong at least until September," a grains trader in Madrid said.

Italian durum wheat prices fell sharply over the past week in the Milan mercantile exchange as producers tried to sell the crop they had left in warehouses at prices that pasta producers thought too expensive.

"Durum wheat prices fell all over Italy but not as much as in Milan which could indicate that prices there had been too high in the past weeks," one dealer said, adding that millers probably have enough in their warehouses to carry them over until the new harvest.
One dealer noted that activity was slim due the market holiday in France on Thursday and many other European countries.
